title: Helix Health Systems — PoC scoping (VPC deployment + eval dataset)
summary: Scoped a short PoC focused on clinical note summarization for internal clinician workflows. Helix emphasized PHI constraints (no PHI to vendor-managed environments, strict retention, limited access) and preference for a VPC deployment with private networking. Agreed to use a small de-identified dataset (or synthetic) with a joint rubric for quality + latency/cost. Redwood to propose an architecture for Redwood Private in Helix’s VPC, clarify logging/audit requirements, and provide a minimal pilot plan with responsibilities and success criteria. Open risk: whether Helix can share any real notes (even de-identified) before legal/privacy review; if not, start with synthetic and validate infra + performance first.
topics: PoC goal and workload selection (clinical note summarization)
Deployment topology (VPC, private endpoints, no public internet)
Security controls: audit logs, encryption/KMS, RBAC/SSO
Success criteria: quality rubric + latency + unit cost
next_steps: Helix (Elena/Jordan) to confirm whether de-identified clinical notes can be used for the PoC and what the approval path is (privacy + legal).
Helix (Tom) to share target cloud (AWS vs Azure), VPC baseline constraints, and preferred connectivity model (PrivateLink/peering).
Redwood (Evan/Fatima) to send a 1–2 page PoC plan: architecture options, data flow diagram, logging/audit log fields, and a proposed eval rubric template.
Redwood (Avery) to schedule a 45-min security-focused follow-up with Helix Security to cover KMS/HSM, retention, and evidence pack items.
Joint to define success thresholds: p95 latency, throughput, and acceptable quality score band; align on which model(s) to test.
action_items: OWNER: Redwood (Evan Scott) — Draft reference architecture for Redwood Private in customer VPC including network boundaries and data flow. DUE: 2025-05-16
OWNER: Helix (Tom Benson) — Provide cloud environment details and network constraints (CIDRs, egress restrictions, PrivateLink/peering preference). DUE: 2025-05-16
OWNER: Helix (Elena Ruiz) — Confirm de-identification standard + retention rules for PoC dataset; confirm whether any PHI can be used at all. DUE: 2025-05-19
OWNER: Redwood (Fatima Noor) — Share eval rubric template and guidance for setting up offline scoring + human review workflow. DUE: 2025-05-19
OWNER: Redwood (Avery Johnson) — Send calendar for security follow-up and include evidence pack request instructions. DUE: 2025-05-15
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-05-14
Time: 1:00 PM ET
Duration: 52 min
Call: Zoom (recorded by Fireflies)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson (AE), Evan Scott (Solutions Engineer), Fatima Noor (SE, Regulated Workloads)
Helix Health Systems: Maya Patel, Jordan Kim, Elena Ruiz, Tom Benson

Auto-generated Summary (Fireflies)
- Discussed PoC scope for internal clinical note summarization and the constraints around PHI.
- Reviewed deployment options and aligned on VPC / private networking requirements.
- Defined next steps for dataset approval, architecture proposal, and security follow-up.


[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is the PoC scoping session. Goal today is we walk away with: one, what workload we’re actually testing, two, what data you can use, and three, what the deployment looks like given your constraints. And then we assign owners so it doesn’t turn into like a, you know, endless email chain.

[00:18] Maya Patel: Sounds good.

[00:19] Jordan Kim: Yep.

[00:21] Avery Johnson: Quick intros for Redwood. I’m Avery, account exec. Evan’s our solutions engineer, he’ll talk architecture. Fatima is our regulated workloads lead, so she’ll keep us honest on what we can and can’t do from a security perspective.

[00:33] Fatima Noor: Hi everyone.

[00:35] Evan Scott: Hey.

[00:37] Avery Johnson: And Maya, you want to intro your side? Just names and what you’re trying to get done.

[00:41] Maya Patel: Sure. Maya Patel. I run clinical applications. This is mostly for an internal clinician workflow—summaries for handoffs, discharge summaries, that kind of thing. Jordan is security engineering, Elena is data governance and privacy, Tom is our platform engineering.

[01:00] Elena Ruiz: Hi.

[01:01] Tom Benson: Hey.

[01:02] Jordan Kim: Hello.

[01:05] Avery Johnson: Great. So Maya, can you level-set the use case? And like, what would make this PoC a “yes” for you.

[01:14] Maya Patel: The narrow thing we want to test is summarizing a clinical note into a structured handoff. We’ve tried a couple approaches with—uh—Azure OpenAI, and our issue is we can’t get our compliance team comfortable with PHI leaving our boundary. Also quality is uneven. For this PoC, if we can show we can run inside our VPC, keep access tight, and have quality that’s not embarrassing, that’s basically the bar.

[01:44] Avery Johnson: Got it. When you say structured handoff, is it like problem list, meds, follow-ups?

[01:49] Maya Patel: Yes. Think: “Active problems,” “Recent labs,” “Pending tests,” “Care team,” “Dispo plan.” And then like 2-3 sentence narrative.

[02:00] Evan Scott: And is it real-time at the point of care, or batch overnight?

[02:04] Maya Patel: Ideally near real-time, but we can start batch. Clinicians hate waiting, but PoC can be a little slower.

[02:12] Evan Scott: Helpful.

[02:13] Avery Johnson: Jordan/Elena, can you share constraints, like hard red lines?

[02:17] Jordan Kim: Yeah. Hard red line is PHI goes to vendor-managed public multi-tenant endpoints. So we can’t do a hosted API where you operate it, basically. We can do something in our VPC, private connectivity only, no public inbound. Egress is restricted. And we need audit logs. Like, we need to be able to answer who accessed what, and when, and from where.

[02:44] Elena Ruiz: And on data: we have to be careful even with “de-identified.” Our policy is de-identification has to meet a specific standard. And retention matters. If the system stores prompts or outputs, that’s a no. Or it needs to be configurable and default to minimal retention.

[03:02] Fatima Noor: That’s super clear. Just to say out loud, Redwood has three modes—hosted, dedicated, and private. For what you’re describing, we’d be looking at Redwood Private. That’s deployed in your environment—VPC or on-prem—so you control networking and keys. We can do “no data retention” configs at the platform layer, but we’ll want to align on what logs you do want, because audit logs are kind of the opposite of “store nothing,” right.

[03:28] Elena Ruiz: Exactly.

[03:29] Jordan Kim: Right, we want logs, but not content.

[03:32] Fatima Noor: Yep—metadata logs without prompt/response bodies. That’s typical.

[03:38] Tom Benson: Quick question: when you say “private,” are we talking a container we run in EKS, or is it like a VM image, or…?

[03:45] Evan Scott: Good question. For the PoC, easiest is Kubernetes on EKS if you have it. We also have options for dedicated nodes and can support VM-based installs, but I’d rather not invent complexity in week one. We can run the inference runtime in your cluster with GPU nodes, and you’ll have a control plane component that’s also inside your network.

[04:08] Tom Benson: We do have EKS. GPU node groups, yes.

[04:11] Evan Scott: Perfect.

[04:12] Avery Johnson: And cloud is AWS then?

[04:14] Tom Benson: Mostly AWS, yes. We have some Azure pockets but for this, AWS.

[04:20] Avery Johnson: Great.

[04:22] Maya Patel: Just to make it explicit, we’re not asking you to sign anything today. We just need to understand what we can test with in 4 to 6 weeks.

[04:31] Avery Johnson: Yep.

[04:33] Fatima Noor: And also, we’ll be careful on language. We don’t say “HIPAA compliant” as a blanket statement. We can support HIPAA-required controls—encryption, access controls, auditability, BAA discussions—depending on the deployment. But we’ll keep it factual.

[04:50] Elena Ruiz: Thank you.

[04:52] Avery Johnson: So, dataset. Elena, what’s feasible? You mentioned de-identified standards.

[04:57] Elena Ruiz: Best case, we can provide a small set of notes that are de-identified under our process. But that requires review. If we can’t in the PoC timeline, we can provide synthetic notes. The issue is synthetic doesn’t validate risk and it doesn’t validate quality in the real world.

[05:18] Maya Patel: Synthetic also doesn’t capture the messiness—abbreviations, weird formatting.

[05:23] Evan Scott: Totally. We can do a phased approach. Phase 0: infra and performance with synthetic. Phase 1: quality eval with de-identified notes once approved.

[05:35] Jordan Kim: For synthetic, where does it live? We cannot upload to your environment.

[05:39] Evan Scott: Under Redwood Private, everything’s in your environment. So your data stays in your VPC. We wouldn’t need it.

[05:46] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[05:48] Elena Ruiz: But if you need us to send prompts for debugging, we can’t.

[05:52] Fatima Noor: Understood. We can troubleshoot via request IDs and metadata, plus model/runtime metrics. If we absolutely need samples, we can do a workflow where you redact and send, but the default should be we don’t ask for content.

[06:08] Avery Johnson: That’s helpful to align now. So, what’s the smallest dataset that’s meaningful? Like 50 notes? 500?

[06:15] Maya Patel: For initial, 200 would be great. But if we can only get 25 through approval, we can start.

[06:24] Evan Scott: For latency and throughput tests, we can generate load without real notes. For quality, even 25-50 can work if we have a consistent rubric.

[06:34] Fatima Noor: Also, we can define an evaluation set with expected outputs—like a “gold summary” created by clinicians. That’s usually the bottleneck.

[06:43] Maya Patel: We can do clinician review on a subset. We already have a QA process in place.

[06:48] Avery Johnson: Great.

[06:50] Tom Benson: Architecture question: do you require outbound internet from the cluster? Our egress is locked down.

[06:56] Evan Scott: For a Private deployment, no, we can run fully private. There are a few things to clarify: model artifacts need to be accessible. We can either pre-load them into an S3 bucket in your account, or you can pull from a private repository through your existing egress controls. For PoC, easiest is you host the artifacts in your S3 and we read from there.

[07:19] Tom Benson: That’s fine.

[07:20] Jordan Kim: Any calls back to your control plane?

[07:23] Evan Scott: Not required. There are optional telemetry hooks, but we can disable external telemetry. Management stays internal.

[07:31] Jordan Kim: We’ll need that in writing.

[07:33] Fatima Noor: Yep, we can provide a data flow diagram and a list of endpoints. That’s part of the PoC plan doc we’ll send.

[07:42] Avery Johnson: Nice.

[07:44] Maya Patel: On models—do we pick models? Or do you push one?

[07:49] Evan Scott: We can recommend based on your constraints: summarization, long-ish context, quality. But we can also test two models. I’d prefer we keep it tight: one baseline model, one alternative.

[08:02] Fatima Noor: And important: we’ll set expectations on GPU needs. Some models are too heavy unless you have a lot of capacity.

[08:10] Tom Benson: We have some A10s and a couple A100s.

[08:13] Evan Scott: Okay. We can size around that.

[08:16] Avery Johnson: Competitor-wise, what are you comparing against? You mentioned Azure OpenAI.

[08:20] Maya Patel: Yeah, Azure OpenAI and also we looked at AWS Bedrock briefly. Bedrock’s governance is closer, but we still have concerns.

[08:29] Jordan Kim: The issue is audit and proof. And we need a clean story on retention.

[08:34] Fatima Noor: Right. For Redwood Private, retention is controlled by you because it’s your infrastructure. But we still need to configure the app to not log content. And we need to be explicit about what is logged—timestamps, user/service identity, model version, token counts, latency, error codes.

[08:55] Jordan Kim: That’s basically what we want. Request ID, caller identity, model, time, outcome.

[09:03] Evan Scott: Do you want logs exported to a SIEM? Splunk? Datadog?

[09:07] Tom Benson: Splunk for security, Datadog for app. But we can start with CloudWatch.

[09:12] Evan Scott: Great.

[09:13] Avery Johnson: Let’s define success criteria. Maya, quality: how do you measure it?

[09:19] Maya Patel: Clinician rating. We do a 1-5 scale on “accurate,” “complete,” and “actionable.” And then we check for hallucinations, especially around meds.

[09:32] Fatima Noor: We should add safety checks: no invented medications, no invented diagnoses. And we can include structured output constraints.

[09:42] Maya Patel: Yes.

[09:43] Evan Scott: Performance: what’s acceptable latency? If this is interactive.

[09:47] Maya Patel: If we could get under 5 seconds for a typical note, that would feel okay. Under 2 seconds would be great.

[09:54] Tom Benson: That depends on note size.

[09:56] Evan Scott: Exactly. We’ll define a “typical” distribution. Also we can do streaming if that helps perceived latency.

[10:06] Maya Patel: Streaming is fine.

[10:08] Avery Johnson: Cost: do you have a target?

[10:10] Maya Patel: Not a strict one. But we can’t spend, like, $3 per summary.

[10:15] Avery Johnson: Fair.

[10:17] Evan Scott: We’ll measure tokens and GPU time. For PoC, we can approximate per-summary cost based on throughput.

[10:25] Jordan Kim: I’m going to keep coming back to data boundaries. Do prompts or responses ever leave the cluster in any scenario?

[10:33] Evan Scott: In the private scenario, no. Unless you explicitly set up an integration that exports content. Default, we do not.

[10:41] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[10:43] Elena Ruiz: And retention—are there caches? Like KV caches? That’s in memory, right?

[10:48] Evan Scott: Yeah, KV cache is in GPU memory for performance. It’s not persistent. It’s tied to the request lifecycle, and then it’s gone.

[10:56] Elena Ruiz: So it’s not written to disk.

[10:58] Evan Scott: Not by default, no.

[11:00] Fatima Noor: We should document that, because people hear “cache” and assume “stored.” We’ll clarify: ephemeral memory, not persisted.

[11:10] Maya Patel: That’s good.

[11:12] Avery Johnson: Timeline-wise, what’s realistic? If we do a 4-week PoC, is that doable given approvals?

[11:18] Elena Ruiz: Privacy review can take two weeks. Legal might take longer if there’s a contract.

[11:24] Avery Johnson: For PoC, we can do it without contract if it’s in your environment and you’re not sharing data with us. But you may still want an NDA. We can be flexible.

[11:35] Jordan Kim: We’ll likely need at least an NDA.

[11:37] Avery Johnson: Okay.

[11:39] Tom Benson: From platform side, we can spin up an EKS namespace and GPU nodes. We’ll need your helm chart or whatever you use.

[11:46] Evan Scott: Yep. We’ll provide deployment instructions and a minimal config. We’ll also specify what permissions the service needs. And for KMS, if you want encryption at rest in EBS or S3, that’s your KMS keys.

[12:02] Jordan Kim: We require KMS encryption at rest across the board.

[12:05] Evan Scott: Great.

[12:07] Fatima Noor: Also, access control. Do you require SSO/SAML for console access? Or is it all API-based?

[12:14] Jordan Kim: Eventually SSO. For PoC, we can do limited admin accounts, but we need RBAC.

[12:21] Evan Scott: We can do RBAC at the platform layer and also rely on your Kubernetes RBAC. We’ll align on the least privilege.

[12:29] Maya Patel: I’m okay if we keep it simple in PoC.

[12:32] Avery Johnson: Great. Let’s talk responsibilities so it doesn’t get fuzzy.

[12:36] Avery Johnson: Redwood responsibilities: we’ll propose architecture, provide install docs, help set up dashboards for latency/cost, and guide eval rubric. Helix responsibilities: provide cloud environment, VPC/networking, GPU capacity, dataset, and clinician review. Does that feel right?

[12:55] Tom Benson: Yes.

[12:56] Maya Patel: Yes.

[12:58] Elena Ruiz: On dataset, yes, but subject to approval.

[13:01] Jordan Kim: And security review. We’ll need a session with your security person.

[13:05] Fatima Noor: Happy to do that.

[13:07] Avery Johnson: Cool.

[13:09] Evan Scott: One more question: do you have any constraints about outbound model updates? Like, are we pinning model versions?

[13:15] Tom Benson: Yes, we need to pin versions. No surprise updates.

[13:19] Evan Scott: Great. We support that. Model version is explicit.

[13:23] Maya Patel: For eval, we also need repeatability. Same prompt, same settings.

[13:28] Evan Scott: Yep.

[13:29] Fatima Noor: Also, we should agree on red teaming / prompt injection boundaries. Even internal, people can paste weird stuff.

[13:37] Maya Patel: We can add that later, but yes.

[13:40] Avery Johnson: Okay, I’m going to jump forward. What are the open risks? I’m hearing one: dataset approval. Two: whether private deployment meets all security requirements without heavy customization. Anything else?

[13:54] Jordan Kim: Audit log completeness. We don’t want “we have logs” but it’s not usable.

[13:59] Evan Scott: Totally. We’ll share sample audit event fields. Things like request ID, timestamp, caller identity, model version, tokens, latency, status. We can also export to your log pipeline.

[14:15] Elena Ruiz: Another risk is outputs containing PHI. Even if input is de-identified, output could re-identify or hallucinate identifiers.

[14:24] Fatima Noor: Great point. We can include constraints in the prompt and add post-processing checks. But the strongest guarantee is your review process + rules in the app layer. We can help propose guardrails.

[14:38] Maya Patel: Yeah, we’ll do clinician review before any production.

[14:41] Avery Johnson: Great.

[14:43] Evan Scott: If helpful, we can define two PoC tracks: track A is infra/performance. Track B is quality. They can run in parallel if dataset comes late.

[14:54] Tom Benson: I like that.

[14:56] Avery Johnson: Okay. Let’s get concrete on deliverables. Evan, can you send a one-pager with architecture and requirements by Friday?

[15:04] Evan Scott: Yes.

[15:06] Avery Johnson: Elena, can you confirm approval steps and whether de-identified notes are possible by early next week?

[15:12] Elena Ruiz: I can confirm the steps. I can’t promise approval by next week, but I can tell you the likely timeline.

[15:19] Avery Johnson: That’s fine.

[15:21] Jordan Kim: And can we schedule the security follow-up? Ideally early next week.

[15:25] Avery Johnson: Yes. I’ll send times.

[15:28] Fatima Noor: In that session we can cover: encryption in transit/at rest, KMS, RBAC, audit logging, retention defaults, and incident response process. And I’ll share what we can provide as evidence under NDA.

[15:42] Jordan Kim: Perfect.

[15:44] Maya Patel: One last question: do we need to build an integration to call the model? Like do you provide an SDK?

[15:50] Evan Scott: There’s a standard REST API. For PoC, you can just use HTTP from a notebook or a small service. We can provide a sample client.

[16:00] Maya Patel: Great.

[16:02] Avery Johnson: Okay, I’m going to recap and then we’ll give you the mic for any gotchas.

[16:07] Avery Johnson: Recap: Use case is clinical note summarization into structured handoff. Deployment is Redwood Private in Helix’s AWS VPC on EKS with GPU node group, private networking, no external telemetry. Data: start synthetic for infra/perf; aim for 25-200 de-identified notes for quality once privacy approves. Logs: metadata-only, no content. Success: clinician ratings + hallucination checks; p95 latency target we’ll define but aim under ~5 seconds for typical note; cost per summary tracked and not crazy. Next steps: Redwood sends PoC plan + architecture; Helix shares VPC constraints; Elena confirms dataset approval path; schedule security session.

[16:54] Tom Benson: That sounds right.

[16:55] Jordan Kim: Yes.

[16:56] Elena Ruiz: Yes.

[16:58] Maya Patel: Yep.

[17:00] Avery Johnson: Anything we missed?

[17:02] Maya Patel: Just that we’ll need a simple way to score outputs and capture feedback. If you have a suggested workflow, that’s helpful.

[17:10] Fatima Noor: We’ll send a rubric template and a lightweight sheet format. Nothing fancy.

[17:15] Avery Johnson: Great. We’ll follow up over email. Thanks all.

[17:20] (Call ends / recording stops)

Note: Transcript is abridged by Fireflies due to crosstalk and repeated sections; timestamps reflect the recording timeline.
